title: Strategies answer different questions

blocks.heading: Strategies answer different questions
blocks.text: Import substitution develops domestic production to replace imports, while export-orientated production is directed primarily towards foreign markets. Strategy, scale and ownership are different dimensions; a locally owned factory can be export-orientated or replace imports. Exports are sales abroad; export-orientated industrialisation is a strategy for building productive capacity around foreign demand. One export sale does not demonstrate that strategy. Compare alternatives against a stated aim using demand, resources, feasibility and who benefits. An ownership label is not evidence of efficiency.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Import substitution
blocks.text: Import substitution means developing domestic production to replace goods previously imported. It may build local productive capacity and reduce dependence on some imports, but needs viable demand, suitable inputs and the ability to produce acceptable goods. In a fictional case, local producers can meet a steady demand for school bags with available skills and material supply. Replacing imported bags may support work and learning. If the domestic process is very costly or still depends on imported inputs, the benefit is narrower than a claim of complete self-sufficiency. Protecting production without improvement may leave users paying more for poor quality.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Export-orientated industry
blocks.text: Export-orientated production means producing goods or services primarily for sale in foreign markets. Access to a larger market can support expansion, but producers must meet delivery, quality and cost requirements and face changes in overseas demand. Confirmed foreign orders can make a larger output worthwhile when transport and inputs are reliable. A producer without a feasible delivery route may fail those orders. Foreign sales can bring earnings, yet dependence on one buyer or product can make local work vulnerable to external changes. Judge the supply and demand conditions rather than assuming a larger market guarantees success.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Large and small scale
blocks.text: Large-scale production can spread some fixed costs and use specialised equipment, while small-scale production may fit limited markets and flexible local tasks. The suitable scale depends on demand, finance, coordination and local resources; greater size alone does not establish lower average cost or wider benefits. A large standardised order may justify equipment that would be underused by a small repair business. A small workshop may adapt products more easily but lack finance for expensive machinery. Compare the same output need, include spare capacity and ask whether a claimed economy of scale actually lowers cost per useful unit.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Multinational investment
blocks.text: Multinational companies operate across countries and may bring finance, technology or links to wider markets. Local gains depend on jobs, training, purchasing, taxation and environmental practice; profits and important decisions may also leave the host economy. An invented investor offering equipment and training can help remove a capacity constraint. If local suppliers are excluded and no skills are transferred, the local link is weaker. Evaluate enforceable arrangements and actual retained benefits. Do not promise that a company will train, hire or buy locally merely because these outcomes are possible.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Local investors and joint enterprises
blocks.text: Local investors organise finance and decisions from within the economy; a joint enterprise combines participation from partners, which may include local and foreign investors. Partners can combine local knowledge with finance or technology, but need workable agreements about decisions, contributions and benefits. Local ownership can support retained earnings and responsiveness to users, but does not remove finance or skill shortages. A joint venture might bridge those gaps, while exposing disagreement over control. Compare a feasible partnership with what the local producer could achieve alone; nationality is not a substitute for evidence about performance.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: State enterprises
blocks.text: State enterprises organise production under state ownership and can pursue strategic services or access goals. They need finance, capable management, maintenance and accountability; public ownership alone does not establish efficient or equitable delivery. A fictional state provider may extend a service to sparsely served communities where commercial returns are limited. It must still sustain the operation and use resources well. Compare reliable access, cost and implementation with a feasible alternative, rather than treating either state or private ownership as an automatic answer.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Public private partnership
blocks.text: A public private partnership is an arrangement in which public and private participants share specified responsibilities for providing infrastructure or a service. It can combine capabilities and resources, but its costs, risks, access requirements and accountability depend on the agreement and its implementation. Public ownership may be retained while a private partner finances or operates a specified facility. That differs from a simple transfer of ownership. A contract that leaves costly failures with the public while excluding low-income users may serve the development aim poorly. Assess responsibilities and realistic enforcement rather than the partnership label.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Choose a strategy against the same aim
blocks.text: Fictional District A wants reliable local employment. A modest domestic market has steady demand and producers can match imported product quality with available skills. A small import-substitution operation is plausible. A much larger export plant would require finance and a reliable shipping route that the district lacks. Under these facts, the smaller operation is better supported, although its potential market is limited. If confirmed foreign demand and a workable route become available, the comparison changes. Strategies can be combined over time: an enterprise may first learn to serve local users and later supply foreign buyers. That is a possible route, not a promise that each stage will occur. For ownership choices, compare who supplies finance, who decides, who bears risk and who retains benefits. The same questions distinguish private investment, state activity and partnership arrangements. Topic 3.1 supplies enterprise and economies of scale; Topic 9.1 develops trade.

blocks.heading: Apply the connection
blocks.text: Compare like aims and feasible alternatives. Trade in Topic 9.1 explains market links; the ownership and scale concepts from Topic 3.1 remain separate dimensions.
